{{Short description|Quantum error correction code}}
{{technical|date=April 2022}}

In [[quantum computing]] and [[quantum communication]], a '''stabilizer code''' is a class of quantum [[code]]s for performing [[quantum error correction]].  The [[toric code]], and [[surface code]]s more generally,<ref>{{cite web|access-date=2024-01-12|title=What is the "surface code" in the context of quantum error correction?|url=https://quantumcomputing.stackexchange.com/questions/2106/what-is-the-surface-code-in-the-context-of-quantum-error-correction|website=Quantum Computing Stack Exchange}}</ref> are types of stabilizer codes considered very important for the practical realization of quantum information processing. In fact, the toric code and surface codes also belong to a special class of stabilizer codes, [[CSS code]]s. An example of a stabilizer code that is not a CSS code is the [[five-qubit error correcting code]].

Stabilizer codes are strikingly similar to classical [[linear block codes]] in their operation and performance. Just as a classical linear block code can be defined by its [[parity-check matrix]], a quantum stabilizer code also has a "parity check" structure defined by its [[Group action (mathematics)#Orbits and stabilizers|stabilizers]]. However, stabilizers for a {{mvar|n}}-qubit code are [[Generalizations of Pauli matrices|{{mvar|n}}-qubit Pauli operator]]s instead of classical {{mvar|n}}-bit strings, and they must all [[Commutative property|commute]] with each other for the code to be valid.

The theory of stabilizer codes allows one to import some classical binary or quaternary codes for use as a quantum code. However, when importing the classical code, it must satisfy the [[dual code|dual-containing]] (or self-orthogonality) constraint. Researchers have found many examples of classical codes satisfying this constraint, but most classical codes do not. Nevertheless, it is still useful to import classical codes in this way. The [[entanglement-assisted stabilizer formalism]] can also overcome this difficulty.

Algebraic-geometry codes provide another source of stabilizer constructions. Matsumoto used algebraic curves to obtain asymptotically good binary stabilizer codes and to improve the Ashikhmin-Litsyn-Tsfasman bound for quantum codes.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Matsumoto |first=Ryutaroh |date=July 2002 |title=Improvement of Ashikhmin-Litsyn-Tsfasman bound for quantum codes |journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory |volume=48 |issue=7 |pages=2122-2124 |doi=10.1109/TIT.2002.1013156 |arxiv=quant-ph/0107129}}</ref>

== Definition ==
The stabilizer formalism is based on the [[Pauli group#Multi-qubit Pauli group|{{mvar|n}}-qubit Pauli group]] {{math|Π<sup>''n''</sup>}}, and extensively uses the facts that [[Self-adjoint operator|Hermitian]] operators (ones with scalar factors {{math|±1}} instead of {{math|±''i''}}) in {{math|Π<sup>''n''</sup>}} have [[eigenvalues]] <math>\pm1</math>, and that two operators in {{math|Π<sup>''n''</sup>}} either [[Commutative property|commute]] or [[anti-commute]].

A ''stabilizer'' of a stabilizer code with {{mvar|n}} physical qubits is an {{mvar|n}}-qubit Pauli operator {{math|''P'' ∈ Π<sup>''n''</sup>}} such that all valid code states <math>|\psi\rangle</math> lie in the {{math|+1}}-[[eigenspace]] of {{mvar|P}}, i.e., {{tmath|P{{!}}\psi\rangle {{=}} {{!}}\psi\rangle}}. A stabilizer code is defined by its stabilizers in the sense that the converse is also true: A state <math>|\psi\rangle</math> is a valid code state for the stabilizer code if and only if {{tmath|P{{!}}\psi\rangle {{=}} {{!}}\psi\rangle}} holds for each stabilizer {{mvar|P}}. Therefore the simultaneous {{math|+1}}-eigenspace of the stabilizers constitutes the ''codespace'' of the stabilizer code.

Any two stabilizers {{mvar|P}} and {{mvar|Q}} must commute and {{mvar|PQ}} must also be a stabilizer. Therefore the stabilizers of a code form the ''stabilizer group'' <math>\mathcal{S}</math>, an [[abelian group|abelian]] [[subgroup]] of {{math|Π<sup>''n''</sup>}}. Conversely, any abelian subgroup of {{math|Π<sup>''n''</sup>}} that does not contain <math>-I^{\otimes n}</math><ref group="note">This condition implies that all members of <math>\mathcal{S}</math> are Hermitian, since an anti-Hermitian element of {{math|Π<sup>''n''</sup>}} squares to <math>-I^{\otimes n}</math>.</ref> is a valid stabilizer group that defines a stabilizer code.

The number of logical qubits encoded in a stabilizer code is determined by the size of the codespace, which is in turn determined by the number of physical qubits and the size of the stabilizer group. For a {{mvar|n}}-qubit stabilizer code encoding {{mvar|k}} logical qubits (denoted as an {{math|<nowiki>[[</nowiki>''n'', ''k'']]}} code), the codespace has {{math|2<sup>''k''</sup>}} dimensions, and the stabilizer group <math>\mathcal{S}</math> has {{math|2<sup>''n'' − ''k''</sup>}} elements. Since all non-unit Hermitian elements of {{math|Π<sup>''n''</sup>}} have [[order (group theory)|order]] 2, <math>\mathcal{S}</math> can be [[Generating set of a group|generated]] by {{math|''n'' − ''k''}} 
independent generators:
:<math>\mathcal{S} = \left\langle g_{1},\ldots,g_{n-k}\right\rangle.</math>
The generators must be independent in the sense that none of them are a product of any number of other generators, or the negation thereof (otherwise they would generate <math>-I^{\otimes n}</math>). They are analogous to the rows of the [[parity-check matrix]] of a classical [[linear block code]].

==Examples==
===Classical repetition code===
{{main|Repetition code}}
As a simple example, the 3-bit {{math|[3, 1, 3]}} classical [[repetition code]] can be regarded as a {{math|<nowiki>[[</nowiki>3, 1, 1]]}} quantum stabilizer code. It encodes {{math|''k'' {{=}} 1}} logical qubit into {{math|''n'' {{=}} 3}} physical qubits, and protects against a single bit-flip error (represented as a Pauli {{mvar|X}} operator {{mvar|X<sub>i</sub>}} in a quantum information context). However, since it does not protect against single-qubit phase-flip errors {{mvar|Z<sub>i</sub>}}, its code distance as a quantum code is {{math|''d'' {{=}} 1}}.

The stabilizer group of the 3-qubit repetition code has {{math|''n'' − ''k'' {{=}} 2}} generators:
:<math>
\begin{array}
[c]{ccc}
g_{1} & = & Z & Z & I\\
g_{2} & = & I & Z & Z\\
\end{array}
</math>
The stabilizer {{math|''g''<sub>1</sub>}} indicates that, if the first and second qubits in a valid code state are both measured in the {{mvar|Z}} basis, the results will always be the same (i.e., the product of {{mvar|Z}} eigenvalues will always be {{math|+1}}). Similarly, {{math|''g''<sub>2</sub>}} indicates that the {{mvar|Z}} basis measurement on the second and third qubits always yield the same result. Unsurprisingly, the codespace of this code is
:<math>\text{Span}(|000\rangle, |111\rangle)</math>.
Usually, the physical state <math>|000\rangle</math> and <math>|111\rangle</math> are identified with the <math>|0\rangle</math> and <math>|1\rangle</math> states of the logical qubit respectively (often written as <math>|\overline{0}\rangle</math> and <math>|\overline{1}\rangle</math> to distinguish them from physical states). As a quantum code, the codespace also includes [[Quantum superposition|superpositions]] of <math>|\overline{0}\rangle</math> and <math>|\overline{1}\rangle</math>, such as <math>|\overline{+}\rangle = |000\rangle + |111\rangle</math> and <math>|\overline{-}\rangle = |000\rangle - |111\rangle</math>. Note that a phase-flip error {{mvar|Z<sub>i</sub>}} on any one physical qubit will change <math>|\overline{+}\rangle</math> to <math>|\overline{-}\rangle</math>, and vice versa.

===Five-qubit code===
{{main|Five-qubit error correcting code}}
An example of a stabilizer code is the five qubit {{math|<nowiki>[[</nowiki>5, 1, 3]]}} stabilizer code. It encodes {{math|''k'' {{=}} 1}} logical qubit into {{math|''n'' {{=}} 5}} physical qubits. Its stabilizer group has {{math|''n'' − ''k'' {{=}} 4}} generators:
:<math>
\begin{array}
[c]{ccccccc}
g_{1} & = & X & Z & Z & X & I\\
g_{2} & = & I & X & Z & Z & X\\
g_{3} & = & X & I & X & Z & Z\\
g_{4} & = & Z & X & I & X & Z
\end{array}
</math>
As we will show later, this code protects against an arbitrary single-qubit error, and thus it has code distance {{math|''d'' {{=}} 3}}.

== Logical operators ==
There are many ways to decompose a {{math|2<sup>''k''</sup>}}-dimension codespace into {{mvar|k}} logical qubits, and one way to specify such a decomposition is by giving Pauli {{mvar|Z}} and {{mvar|X}} operators for each logical qubit. For stabilizer codes, there exists decompositions where these logical {{mvar|Z}} and {{mvar|X}} operators are also elements of {{math|Π<sup>''n''</sup>}}.

By definition, a logical operator {{mvar|P}} must map a valid code state <math>|\psi\rangle</math> into a valid code state {{tmath|P{{!}}\psi\rangle}}. This means that for each stabilizer {{mvar|S}}, <math>SP|\psi\rangle = P|\psi\rangle = PS|\psi\rangle</math> (the second equality holds since <math>|\psi\rangle</math> is itself a valid code state), which is always true when {{mvar|P}} and {{mvar|S}} commute and never true when they anti-commute. Therefore the set of valid logical operators in {{math|Π<sup>''n''</sup>}} is {{tmath|C(\mathcal{S})}}, the [[centralizer]] of <math>\mathcal{S}</math> (i.e., the subgroup of elements that commute with all members of {{tmath|\mathcal{S}<!-- -->}}, also known as the commutant).

However, not all these logical operators act non-trivially on the logical qubit. In particular, since <math>\mathcal{S}</math> is an abelian subgroup, <math>\mathcal{S}</math> is also contained in {{tmath|C(\mathcal{S})}}. In fact, when {{tmath|S \in \mathcal{S}<!-- -->}}, {{tmath|S{{!}}\psi\rangle {{=}} {{!}}\psi\rangle}}, meaning that {{mvar|S}} implements the logical identity operator <math>I^{\otimes k}</math>. Furthermore, for any other logical operator {{mvar|P}}, {{mvar|PS}} acts identically to {{mvar|P}} on the code state, and thus they implement the same logical operator. Factoring out this equivalence gives the [[quotient group]] {{tmath|C(\mathcal{S}) / \mathcal{S}<!-- -->}}, which is [[isomorphic]] to {{math|Π<sup>''k''</sup>}}. Therefore all {{mvar|k}}-qubit logical Pauli operators can be chosen to be {{mvar|n}}-qubit physical Pauli operators.

To explicitly specify the logical qubit decomposition, one usually chooses logical operators {{math|{{overline|''Z''<sub>1</sub>}}, {{overline|''X''<sub>1</sub>}}, ..., {{overline|''Z''<sub>''k''</sub>}}, {{overline|''X''<sub>''k''</sub>}} ∈ Π<sup>''n''</sup>}}. Each of these operators {{mvar|{{overline|Z<sub>i</sub>}}}} or  {{mvar|{{overline|X<sub>i</sub>}}}} is a ''representative'' for the equivalence class <math>\overline{Z_i}\mathcal{S}</math> or <math>\overline{X_i}\mathcal{S}</math> implementing the same logical operator. These operators need to satisfy the following conditions:
* {{math|{{overline|''Z''<sub>1</sub>}}, {{overline|''X''<sub>1</sub>}}, ..., {{overline|''Z''<sub>''k''</sub>}}, {{overline|''X''<sub>''k''</sub>}}, ''g''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''g''<sub>''n'' − ''k''</sub>}} are ''all'' independent: The product of any nonempty subset of these operators cannot be a scalar multiple of <math>I^{\otimes n}</math>.
* Among {{math|{{overline|''Z''<sub>1</sub>}}, {{overline|''X''<sub>1</sub>}}, ..., {{overline|''Z''<sub>''k''</sub>}}, {{overline|''X''<sub>''k''</sub>}}, ''g''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''g''<sub>''n'' − ''k''</sub>}}, the only pairs that anti-commute are {{mvar|{{overline|Z<sub>i</sub>}}}} and  {{mvar|{{overline|X<sub>i</sub>}}}} for the same {{mvar|i}}. Other pairs — two logical operators on different logical qubits, one logical operator and one stabilizer generator, or two stabilizer generators — all commute.

=== Examples ===
For the 3-qubit repetition code described above, the stabilizer generators (repeated for convenience) and logical operator representatives can be chosen as:
:<math>
\begin{array}
[c]{ccc}
g_{1} & = & Z & Z & I\\
g_{2} & = & I & Z & Z\\
\overline{Z} & = & Z & I & I\\
\overline{X} & = & X & X & X
\end{array}
</math>
Other single-qubit {{mvar|Z}} operators are alternative implementations of the logical {{mvar|Z}} operator: {{math|''Z''<sub>2</sub> {{=}} {{overline|''Z''}}''g''<sub>1</sub>}}, {{math|''Z''<sub>3</sub> {{=}} {{overline|''Z''}}''g''<sub>1</sub>''g''<sub>2</sub>}}. This is consistent with the above observation that any single-qubit phase-flip error changes <math>|\overline{+}\rangle</math> to <math>|\overline{-}\rangle</math>, and vice versa. It is also straightforward to check that applying {{math|{{overline|''X''}} {{=}} ''XXX''}}, i.e., bit-flipping all three qubits, changes <math>|\overline{0}\rangle</math> to <math>|\overline{1}\rangle</math>, and vice versa.

For the five-qubit code, the logical operator representatives are usually chosen as:
:<math>
\begin{array}
[c]{ccccccc}
g_{1} & = & X & Z & Z & X & I\\
g_{2} & = & I & X & Z & Z & X\\
g_{3} & = & X & I & X & Z & Z\\
g_{4} & = & Z & X & I & X & Z\\
\overline{Z} & = & Z & Z & Z & Z & Z\\
\overline{X} & = & X & X & X & X & X
\end{array}
</math>
Note, however, that these are not the logical operator representative candidates with the lowest weight (number of non-{{mvar|I}} Pauli factors). For example, {{math|{{overline|''Z''}}''g''<sub>1</sub> {{=}} −''YIIYZ''}} has weight 3.

== Stabilizer error-correction conditions ==

One of the fundamental notions in quantum error correction theory is that it
suffices to correct a [[Discrete set|discrete]] error set with [[Support (mathematics)|support]] in the Pauli group
<math>\Pi^{n}</math>. Suppose that the errors affecting an
encoded quantum state are a subset <math>\mathcal{E}</math> of the Pauli group <math>\Pi^{n}</math>:
:<math>\mathcal{E}\subset\Pi^{n}.</math>

Because <math>\mathcal{E}</math> and <math>\mathcal{S}</math> are both subsets of  <math>\Pi^{n}</math>, an error <math>E\in\mathcal{E}</math> either [[Commutative property|commute]]s or [[anti-commute]]s with any particular element <math>S \in \mathcal{S}</math>. If {{mvar|E}} anti-commutes with an element {{mvar|S}}, then <math>SE|\psi\rangle = -ES|\psi\rangle = -E|\psi\rangle</math> which means that <math>E|\psi\rangle</math> is in the {{math|−1}}-[[eigenspace]] of {{mvar|S}} rather than the {{math|+1}}-[[eigenspace]], and thus {{mvar|E}} is detectable by [[quantum measurement|measuring]] {{mvar|S}}. Actually it suffices to measure each stabilizer generator {{mvar|g}}, since if {{mvar|E}} commutes with every {{mvar|g}}, then {{mvar|E}} will also commute with the product of any number of them. In this case <math>E \in C(\mathcal{S})</math> is a logical operator and thus cannot be detected by the code.

However, <math>E \in \mathcal{S}</math> is again a special case, where {{mvar|E}} implements the logical identity operator: Even though it is not detectable, it also does not corrupt the encoded state. This also holds for any scalar multiple of <math>E \in \mathcal{S}</math>, since a [[List of quantum logic gates#Identity gate and global phase|global phase]] has no physical effect. We define an ''undetectable logical error'' {{mvar|E}} as one that is undetectable but does corrupt the encoded state, i.e.,
:<math>E \in C(\mathcal{S}) \setminus \{+1, +i, -1, -i\} \otimes \mathcal{S} = C(\mathcal{S}) \setminus C(C(\mathcal{S})).</math>
The equality above gives an alternative characterization of an undetectable logical error {{mvar|E}}: {{mvar|E}} must commute with all stabilizers, but not with all logical operators. This characterization is often more convenient since one only need to check commutativity with the generators {{math|{{overline|''Z''<sub>1</sub>}}, {{overline|''X''<sub>1</sub>}}, ..., {{overline|''Z''<sub>''k''</sub>}}, {{overline|''X''<sub>''k''</sub>}}, ''g''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''g''<sub>''n'' − ''k''</sub>}}, instead of solving a system of linear equations to determine if {{mvar|E}} is the product of some subset of {{math|{''g''<sub>''i''</sub>}<!-- -->}} up to global phase.

Operationally, each stabilizer generator {{mvar|g}} can be measured via a [[parity measurement]] without disturbing states in the codespace. The combination of results of measuring each {{mvar|g}} is known as the ''syndrome'' <math>\mathbf{r}</math>, represented as a binary vector <math>\mathbf{r}</math> with length <math>n-k</math> whose elements indicate whether the error {{mvar|E}} commutes or anti-commutes with each stabilizer generator {{mvar|g}}.

=== Knill–Laflamme conditions ===
When using a stabilizer code as an error ''correction'' code, one must also choose a correction {{math|''E''<sub>1</sub><sup>†</sup>}}<ref group="note">Although Pauli errors are all [[Self-adjoint operator|self-adjoint]], here we use notations that align with the more general quantum error-correction theory.</ref> for each syndrome. If there exists another possible error {{math|''E''<sub>2</sub>}} with the same syndrome as {{math|''E''<sub>1</sub>}}, then after correction there may be a residual error {{math|''E''<sub>1</sub><sup>†</sup>''E''<sub>2</sub>}}. The condition that {{math|''E''<sub>2</sub>}} has the same syndrome as {{math|''E''<sub>1</sub>}} is equivalent to that {{math|''E''<sub>1</sub><sup>†</sup>''E''<sub>2</sub>}} is undetectable, i.e., <math>E_1^\dagger E_2 \in C(\mathcal{S})</math>. However, if {{math|''E''<sub>1</sub><sup>†</sup>''E''<sub>2</sub>}} does not corrupt the logical qubits, then the error correction will be successful anyway. Therefore, a stabilizer code can perfectly correct a set of Pauli errors <math>\mathcal{E}</math> as long as there does not exist <math>E_1, E_2 \in \mathcal{E}</math> such that {{math|''E''<sub>1</sub><sup>†</sup>''E''<sub>2</sub>}} is an undetectable logical error.<ref group="note">In most cases, <math>\mathcal{E}</math> is defined in a way such that it includes <math>I^{\otimes n}</math>, to be chosen as the correction when no error has happened. This way, the no-error case does not need to be treated specially.</ref>

=== Examples ===
The 3-qubit repetition code can correct single-qubit bit-flip errors, which means that it satisfies the error-correction conditions for <math>\mathcal{E} = \{I, X_1, X_2, X_3\}</math>. Indeed, the only undetectable logical error that consists only of {{mvar|I}} and {{mvar|X}} is {{mvar|XXX}} with weight 3, and the product of two errors in <math>\mathcal{E}</math> . This can also be verified by explicitly checking the corrections corresponding to each syndrome:

{| class="wikitable"
! Syndrome !! Correction
|-
| {{math|+1, +1}} || {{mvar|I}}
|-
| {{math|−1, +1}} || {{math|''X''<sub>1</sub>}}
|-
| {{math|−1, −1}} || {{math|''X''<sub>2</sub>}}
|-
| {{math|+1, −1}} || {{math|''X''<sub>3</sub>}}
|}

The five-qubit code can correct any single-qubit error, i.e., it satisfies the error-correction conditions for <math>\mathcal{E} = \{I, X_i, Y_i, Z_i\}</math> ({{math|1 + 5 × 3 {{=}} 16}} distinct errors). This can be verified either by showing that all undetectable logical errors of this code has weight at least 3, or by explicitly checking the {{math|2<sup>4</sup> {{=}} 16}} syndromes. For the five-qubit code again each syndrome corresponds to one error in <math>\mathcal{E}</math>, although this is not typical for stabilizer codes: For codes like the [[surface code]] with high code distances and relatively low-weight stabilizers, one syndrome will usually correspond to many correctable errors that differ from each other by stabilizers.

== Relation between Pauli group and binary vectors ==
{{main|Pauli group#Binary vector representation}}

The Pauli group has a [[Pauli group#Binary vector representation|binary vector representation]] based on the following mapping:
:{{tmath|
I \to 00, \; X \to 01, \; Y \to 11, \; Z \to 10.
}}
This mapping maps {{tmath|\Pi^n}} to vectors in {{tmath|(\mathbb{Z}_{2})^{2n} }}, such that multiplication of Pauli operators is equivalent to addition of binary vectors up to a global phase. Furthermore, {{tmath|(\mathbb{Z}_{2})^{2n} }} can be equipped with a [[symplectic algebra]], such that the [[symplectic product]] of two binary vectors indicate whether the corresponding Pauli operators commute.

The above binary representation and symplectic algebra are especially useful in making the relation between classical linear [[error correction]] and quantum stabilizer codes more explicit. In the language of [[symplectic vector space]]s, a [[Symplectic vector space#Subspaces|symplectic]] subspace corresponds to a [[direct sum]] of Pauli algebras (i.e., encoded qubits), while an [[Symplectic vector space#Subspaces|isotropic]] subspace corresponds to a set of stabilizers.
